dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Feeding and Eating Disorders — Anorexia Nervosa
summary: Persistent restriction of food intake that keeps weight well below a healthy level for the person, driven by a strong fear of weight gain and by self-judgment centered on shape and weight. Some clients also binge or purge. The client may not see the low weight as a problem. This condition has one of the highest mortality rates in mental health, through medical complications and suicide, so medical monitoring is part of care from the first contact. Outpatient eating-disorder-focused therapy (such as CBT-E, focal psychodynamic therapy or MANTRA) works for many adults; lower weights or medical instability need a higher level of care. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how long restriction and weight loss have gone on and what the weight trend has been. See DSM-5-TR for duration and severity guidance; medical risk does not wait for a duration threshold.

ruleOuts.label: Thyroid, gastrointestinal and endocrine illness
ruleOuts.note: Hyperthyroidism, diabetes, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and other illnesses can cause weight change or eating changes; coordinate a medical work-up.

ruleOuts.label: Medication and substance effects
ruleOuts.note: Stimulants, some antidepressants, antipsychotics and other medicines change appetite and weight. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Depression and other mental health conditions
ruleOuts.note: Appetite loss in depression, food avoidance from fear of choking (ARFID) or contamination fears (OCD) can look similar; ask what drives the eating change.

specifiers.label: Restricting or binge-eating/purging type (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Sets the ICD-10-CM code family (F50.01x or F50.02x); the last character records severity or remission.

differentials.label: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Restriction comes from fear of choking, vomiting or sensory dislike, not from fear of weight gain.

differentials.label: Bulimia nervosa
differentials.distinguishing: Binges with compensation at a weight in or above the healthy range.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Appetite loss without fear of weight gain or shape concern.

differentials.label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Food rules driven by contamination fears or rituals rather than weight.

comorbidities.label: Depression
comorbidities.note: Common, and low weight itself worsens mood; screen with the PHQ-9 and ask about suicide.

comorbidities.label: OCD
comorbidities.note: Rituals and rigidity often co-occur; assess separately.

comorbidities.label: Anxiety disorders
comorbidities.note: Anxiety often comes before and alongside; screen with the GAD-7.

interventions.name: Medical assessment and monitoring (first step)
interventions.evidence: NICE NG69 sets out physical monitoring for people with eating disorders; Arcelus et al. (2011) found raised mortality across eating disorders.
interventions.note: Refer to a physician for vital signs, labs and ECG as indicated; agree when to go to the emergency department.

interventions.name: Enhanced CBT for eating disorders (CBT-E)
interventions.evidence: Fairburn et al. (2009) tested transdiagnostic CBT-E; NICE NG69 lists eating-disorder-focused CBT for adults with anorexia.
interventions.note: Regular eating, weight monitoring and work on shape concern; best delivered by trained clinicians.

interventions.name: Focal psychodynamic therapy
interventions.evidence: In the ANTOP trial (Zipfel et al., 2014), focal psychodynamic therapy and CBT-E both helped outpatients with anorexia.
interventions.note: Refer to clinicians trained in the approach.

interventions.name: Dietitian collaboration
interventions.evidence: NICE NG69 recommends a team approach with dietetic input.
interventions.note: Coordinate a meal plan with a dietitian experienced in eating disorders.

interventions.name: Safety planning
interventions.evidence: Suicide risk is raised in anorexia.
interventions.note: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and build a safety plan; this app never rates risk.

culturalNotes: Eating disorders occur across all genders, body sizes, ages, ethnic groups and income levels. Do not rule one out because the client is male, older, a person of color or in a larger body.

Food, fasting, body ideals and family meals carry cultural and religious meaning. Ask about religious fasting, cultural foods and family roles before planning meals, and adapt the plan rather than asking the client to drop practices that matter to them.
Weight stigma in health care is common. Use weight-neutral, respectful language and ask before weighing; consider blind weights where clinically appropriate.
Food insecurity can drive restriction followed by overeating. Ask about access to food and connect the client with food resources where needed.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.
If the client wants faith or spiritual practice included, follow their lead and get informed consent first (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors); never impose beliefs.

redFlagRules.message: Medical warning signs related to eating are documented. Eating disorders carry real medical risk: arrange a same-day or urgent medical assessment (vital signs, electrolytes, ECG as indicated) and agree on a medical monitoring plan.

Suicidal thoughts or self-harm are documented in this input. Ask directly about intent, plan and access to means, follow your crisis protocol and build a safety plan with the client; this app never rates risk.
